title: Comments of Google LLC on Midcontinent Independent System Operator Inc.’s Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads Proposal under ER26-3650.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                         )
 Midcontinent Independent System Operator                )           Docket No. ER26-3650-000
 Inc.                                                    )
                                                         )

                                  COMMENTS OF GOOGLE LLC

          Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission”),1 Google LLC (“Google”) submits these comments on

Midcontinent Independent System Operator Inc.’s (“MISO”) Interconnection Reliability

Requirements for Large Loads Proposal (“IRR Proposal”). Google supports the proposal as a

reasonable and responsible step to bolster the near-term reliability of the nation’s electric grid.

          Ensuring electric reliability must continue to be job number one. That responsibility has

become increasingly complex, in large part due to the addition of large loads that may exhibit

different operating characteristics than other loads.          Google therefore commends MISO for

prioritizing the reliability of the transmission system and working proactively to identify and

mitigate the risks that certain Large Loads can pose to the power grid. In addition, Google supports

MISO’s pragmatic approach to these issues, including its reasonable grandfathering of existing

customers in a manner that respects reliance interests and investments made under the rules in

effect at the time. An approach along the lines proposed in this proceeding is consistent with

Google’s approach to responsible energy growth.2



    1
        18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2026).
    2
      See Amanda Peterson Corio, Supporting the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge: Google's Approach for
Responsible Energy Growth, Google: The Keyword (Mar. 4, 2026), https://blog.google/innovation-and-
ai/infrastructure-and-cloud/global-network/affordability-pledge-responsible-energy-growth.
              At the same time, while Google supports this filing, additional work is needed to further

     refine MISO’s approach to reliability issues associated with new Large Loads. For example, the

     best way to ensure the reliability of the system is to tie any regulations or requirements to the

     electrical characteristics of the load rather than the specific type of end use they constitute. In

     other words, regulators should focus on imposing obligations based on the reliability challenges

     associated with a particular load (e.g., ramp rate, voltage sensitivity, etc.) rather than the nature of

     the retail customer (e.g., data center, arc furnace, etc.). In addition, several aspects of the IRR

     Proposal have yet to come into focus, either because they will be specified in the MISO Business

     Practice Manuals (“BPM”) or because the proposed tariff language gives MISO significant

     discretion over how it will implement the IRR Proposal. Those implementation questions will go

     a long way in determining the effectiveness and administrability of the IRR Proposal.

I.       COMMENTS

             As noted, Google supports the IRR Proposal. It offers the following observations and

     suggestions as MISO and the Commission continue to refine their approach to addressing the

     reliability implications of load growth driven by new Large Loads.

             A. Grandfathering Existing Loads Is Important and Consistent with Commission
                Policy

             Google supports the grandfathering provisions in the IRR Proposal, which provide

     important commercial certainty to entities seeking to invest in the MISO region .                  The

     grandfathering paradigm is also consistent with Commission policy and analogous large load

     regulatory frameworks for other Independent System Operators (“ISOs”)/Regional Transmission

     Organizations (“RTOs”). Under the IRR Proposal, the extent to which MISO will regulate Large

     Loads varies depending on the date on which service to the Large Load begins, whether

     transmission projects or upgrades associated with the Large Load have been approved by the


                                                           -2-
 MISO Board in MTEP, and when transmission projects or upgrades associated with the Large

Load are submitted to the MISO EPR process. 3 For example, Large Loads with a transmission

service commencement date on or prior to December 4, 2026—i.e., the proposed effective date of

the IRR Proposal—will not be subject to certain IRR regulations. 4

           Data centers have operated safely and reliably within the MISO footprint for years (and in

some cases, decades). Google applauds MISO for crafting regulations that reflect its considerable

experience operating a grid that has long provided service to data center loads, rather than imposing

on those loads a new regulatory regime meant to mitigate risks that those loads have never

presented.

           The grandfathering provisions do more than just reflect MISO’s experience to date; they

also provide commercial certainty for parties that have already invested in electrical and digital

infrastructure in MISO and send an important signal to prospective investors that they can rely on

the regulatory landscape to remain predictable. This, in turn, creates the certainty necessary to

deploy capital needed to upgrade digital and electrical infrastructure, including through

investments that help make data centers better grid citizens. As Google has emphasized, during

this time of rapid transformation, regulations that create uncertainty or raise the risk that

investments made in reliance on the rules in effect at the time will be rendered obsolete decrease

companies’ appetite to make those investments voluntarily.5                 As such, greater regulatory

uncertainty can lead to impaired reliability if it prevents companies from making the investments




    3
      Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Reliability Requirements for Large Loads, Docket No. ER26-3650-
000, 13-14 (filed Aug. 28, 2026) (“Transmittal”).
    4
        Id. at 14.
    5
    See generally PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest of Google LLC, Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (filed Sept. 3,
2026).

                                                         -3-
 that will go above and beyond to ensure that the grid remains safe and reliable. Grandfathering

provisions, like the ones in the IRR Proposal, respect existing reliance interests and signal to

investors and developers that the regulatory ground beneath them is less likely to shift

unexpectedly.

         Moreover, respecting reliance interests, including through existing contracts and

commercial arrangements, is consistent with the Commission’s guidance in the MISO Large Load

Show Cause Order where the Commission encouraged MISO to “(a) propose a reasonable

implementation period to ensure minimal disruption to such existing commercial arrangements,

and (b) allow a reasonable amount of time to finalize ongoing agreements that are nearing

completion as of the date such Tariff provisions are filed with the Commission. Such proposed

Tariff revisions should include a reasonable effective date that accommodates such considerations

regarding these existing commercial arrangements.” 6 The IRR Proposal grandfathering provisions

do just that. Projects that begin operating before the effective date of the IRR Proposal will be

subject to the regulations in effect when those projects were conceived, not the entirely new IRR

regulatory regime, and projects that are verifiably in progress will only be subject to a subset of

the IRR regulations, thus ensuring minimal disruption.

         The grandfathering provisions in the IRR Proposal are also consistent with transition

mechanisms that the Commission has approved for similar regulations in SPP. SPP’s HILLS

construct imposes reliability requirements on large loads, which include load forecasting

provisions, remote capability to disconnect load from the transmission system, installation of

phasor measurement units for real-time load data, and ride-through requirements.7 SPP’s large



   6
       Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 5 (2026).
   7
       Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031, at PP 18-20, 63 (2026).

                                                         -4-
 load reliability requirements similarly do not apply to existing loads. 8 Google urges the

Commission to note the importance of this approach and encourage any other regions considering

similar measures to follow suit and adopt an approach that, as noted above, facilitates the

investment in the reliability measures that the country badly needs.

           At the same time, as noted above, ensuring electric reliability must remain job number

one. To that end, MISO has included important “notwithstanding” language in the grandfathering

provisions of the IRR Proposal,9 which allows it to continue monitoring the operational risks

introduced by certain large loads and modify its approach where necessary to address reliability

risks. In so doing, MISO has struck an important balance that preserves reliance interests while

also preserving its ability to adjust its approach as needed to ensure reliability .

           B. Large Loads Should Be Classified and Regulated Based on Their Objective
              Electrical Characteristics Rather than the Function they Perform

           The IRR Proposal regulates Large Loads based on the function they perform—e.g.,

computation—rather than their operational characteristics and their effects on the grid. This means

that MISO may end up regulating some Large Loads that do not pose a reliability risk to the

transmission system while excluding non-data center loads that pose some of the same risks.

Under the IRR Proposal, MISO would subject Computational Loads, which it defines as “Large

Load comprised of 25 MW or more of Demand from information technology equipment, such as

servers, storage, and networking hardware,”10 to more onerous regulatory requirements than Large

Loads, which MISO defines as loads over 50 MW at a single substation behind one or more



    8
       Id. P 10 (“A load may be categorized as a HILL after the initial effective date of Attachment BA of the Tariff.”);
id. P 10 n.23 (“Existing loads will not be considered HILLs or be subject to the requirements of Attachment BA unless
they seek to increase load and otherwise meet the definitional requirements.”).

    10

                                                               -5-
 Point(s) of Withdrawal from the Transmission System.11 Specifically, Large Loads would need to

comply with visibility requirements while Computational Loads would also need to comply with

ramp, PMU, and ride-through requirements. As MISO explains, “[d]efining Computational Load

supports a more targeted and risk-informed approach, rather than applying the same requirements

to all Large Loads regardless of facility type or operating behavior.”12

           As noted above, Google believes reliability requirements like those in this proposal are

important and need to be implemented promptly. Nevertheless, by proposing a scheme that turns

on the function that a facility performs rather than on its electrical behavior, MISO has, in fact,

created an approach that “appl[ies] the same requirements . . . regardless of . . . operating behavior.”

To see why this is the case, consider industrial loads beyond data centers (e.g., arc furnaces,

cryogenic facilities, hydrogen electrolyzers, etc.), which can exhibit identical electrical behaviors

as certain data centers but would escape the ramp, PMU, and ride-through requirements in the IRR

Proposal. At the same time, data centers that do not exhibit high-risk behaviors—e.g., because

they have made investments or adopted operational protocols to reduce impact on the grid—would

be regulated as Computational Loads. An approach that regulates loads based on their risks to and

effects on the grid would not only be a more efficient system of regulation; it would also

incentivize data center operators to make additional investments needed to mitigate or eliminate

those effects entirely—a win-win situation for both customers and grid operators more generally.

           C. The Success of the IRR Proposal Will Depend on Details that Will Be Included in
             MISO’s Manuals

          MISO has deferred critical details of the IRR regulatory paradigm—e.g., the 30

MW/minute ramp calculation methodology, voltage ride-through curve specifications, and

deviation penalties—to its Business Practice Manuals. As such, the IRR Proposal is best described

as a high-level framework rather than a comprehensive regulatory regime, which makes it difficult

to evaluate whether the IRR Proposal will achieve its stated goals and, relatedly, the extent to

which Large Loads will be able to comply with its requirements. Google recognizes that some of

the terms and requirements that MISO has left unspecified are technical implementation details

that should be set forth in the Business Practice Manuals. We urge MISO to work closely with

stakeholders in fleshing out those details.

          At the same time, the IRR Proposal gives MISO open-ended authority to impose what

amounts to penalties on Large Loads that fail to comply with various new requirements (e.g.,

modeling, data, telemetry, etc.), which raises a particular risk of running afoul of the rule of reason.

Under the rule of reason, practices that “affect rates and service significantly,” “are realistically

susceptible of specification,” and “are not so generally understood in any contractual arrangement

as to render recitation superfluous” must be filed with the Commission, not housed in Business

Practice Manuals and the like. 13 The Commission has previously found that penalty provisions

that significantly affect the conditions of transmission service must be included in a transmission

provider’s tariff.14




    13
         City of Cleveland v. FERC, 773 F.2d 1368, 1376 (D.C. Cir. 1985) (emphasis removed).
    14
      See California Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 175 FERC ¶ 61,245, at P 166 (2021), order on reh’g, 178 FERC
¶ 61,180 (2022).

                                                         -7-
           The penalty authority in the IRR Proposal could do just that. Specifically, for transmission

customers that do not comply with the regulatory requirements in the IRR Proposal, MISO will

have unbounded discretion to delay the commencement date for transmission service to the new

Large Loads, impose operational limitations, or impose other remediation actions necessary to

maintain the reliability of the transmission system.15 In other words, MISO is reserving to itself

the power to penalize customers by imposing conditions on transmission service. While MISO

itself acknowledges, “clarity is required as to potential consequences in the event a party fails to

comply with applicable requirements,”16 it has yet to provide such clarity, and Google urges MISO

to do so promptly and with the predictability necessary to avoid rule of reason concerns.

          D. The Breadth of Certain Provisions Could Make it Difficult for Entities to Comply
             with the IRR Proposal

          Finally, Google is concerned that some provisions in the IRR Proposal are framed so

broadly that it will be difficult, if not impossible, for regulated entities to comply. Most notably,

the IRR Proposal gives MISO the right to audit information “including, but not limited to,

information related to the registration, claimed capacity, operations, modeling, inverter settings,

metering, settlements, Large Load Equipment, and/or any other information related to the

participation of the Large Load under this Tariff.”17 While Google believes that MISO should

have the audit rights necessary to ensure that entities are complying with its tariff —after all, the

reliability of the grid depends on it—giving MISO such unbounded and undefined powers could

complicate compliance for Large Loads in the region. In the absence of limits on the information

that MISO can request, Large Loads will be required to retain a nearly limitless amount of

   information. MISO should be able to access any information it needs to ensure that Large Loads

  (and the transmission customers taking service on their behalf) are complying with reliability

  requirements. That said, a regime under which entities need to retain everything because MISO

  can ask for anything will become unduly burdensome, unworkable in practice, and actually

  complicate the process of complying with these critical regulations.

II.     Conclusion

              Google supports the IRR Proposal, which will help MISO ensure reliability in this era of

  rapid load growth. But the work cannot end here. Eventually, the Commission should ensure that,

  where appropriate, the reliability requirements imposed by ISOs/RTOs align with the large load

  reliability standards that it has directed the North American Electric Reliability Corporation to

  develop.18 This will help to avoid a patchwork of reliability requirements across ISOs/RTOs,

  improving reliability and reducing compliance costs.
